N-mixture models with mvgam

Nicholas J Clark

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/articles/nmix.Rmd
nmix.Rmd

A count of animals mixes the number present with the chance of detecting each one. A single survey cannot tell a large population counted poorly from a small one counted well. N-mixture models separate the two with replicate visits made while the population is closed to change (Royle 2004). The mean of the replicate counts reflects abundance times detection. Their spread reflects detection alone.

The nmix() family places this model inside an mvgam state-space model. The latent abundance can then follow a temporal trend, respond to covariates through trend_formula and be forecast. This article simulates yearly surveys of four species whose abundances respond to temperature in different ways, while wind lowers the chance of detecting them. One model recovers each species’ abundance in every year, the two covariate effects and a forecast of the counts.

The model

Species ss is counted on visit rr in year tt. Each count is a binomial draw from the Ns,tN_{s,t} individuals present:

ys,t,r∼Binomial(Ns,t,ps,t,r)Ns,t∼Poisson(λs,t)log⁡λs,t=αs+fs(tempt)+zs,tzs,t∼Normal(ϕszs,t−1,σs)logit(ps,t,r)=γs+δwinds,t,r\begin{align*} y_{s,t,r} & \sim \text{Binomial}(N_{s,t}, p_{s,t,r}) \\ N_{s,t} & \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{s,t}) \\ \log \lambda_{s,t} & = \alpha_s + f_s(\text{temp}_t) + z_{s,t} \\ z_{s,t} & \sim \text{Normal}(\phi_s z_{s,t-1}, \sigma_s) \\ \text{logit}(p_{s,t,r}) & = \gamma_s + \delta \, \text{wind}_{s,t,r} \end{align*}

Each species has its own smooth response fsf_s to temperature. Its AR(1) state zsz_s absorbs the year-to-year change that temperature leaves unexplained. Each species also has its own detection intercept γs\gamma_s. All species share one wind effect δ\delta on detection.

Because Hamiltonian Monte Carlo cannot sample the integer Ns,tN_{s,t}, mvgam sums the likelihood over every value of NN from the largest count up to a cap. Stan then samples only continuous parameters. The Stan User’s Guide chapter on latent discrete parameters describes the technique.

The data

To compare estimates with known abundances, we simulate four species surveyed on five visits in each of 20 years. The first species’ abundance rises with temperature and levels off. The second peaks at intermediate temperatures. The third declines. The fourth has a weak U shape. On every visit, the detection probability falls with wind speed.

set.seed(11)
n_sp <- 4
n_year <- 20
n_visit <- 5
species <- paste0("sp_", seq_len(n_sp))

# A yearly temperature index with mean 0 and SD 1
temp <- round(as.numeric(scale(
  cumsum(rnorm(n_year, 0, 0.6)) + rnorm(n_year)
)), 2)

# AR(1) deviations in log abundance that temperature leaves unexplained
z <- matrix(0, n_year, n_sp)
for (t in 2:n_year) z[t, ] <- 0.6 * z[t - 1, ] + rnorm(n_sp, 0, 0.2)

# Each species' response to temperature on the log scale: a
# saturating rise, a hump, a decline and a weak U
temp_effect <- cbind(
  0.8 * tanh(1.5 * temp),
  0.6 - 0.6 * temp^2,
  -0.5 * temp,
  0.2 * temp^2 - 0.2
)

# Abundance N each year, around baselines of 30, 12, 20 and 10
log_lambda <- sweep(temp_effect + z, 2, log(c(30, 12, 20, 10)), "+")
N <- matrix(rpois(n_year * n_sp, exp(log_lambda)), n_year, n_sp)

# Logit detection intercept of each species
det_sp <- rnorm(n_sp, 0.3, 0.4)

# One row per visit, with wind speed recorded on each
dat <- expand.grid(visit = seq_len(n_visit), time = seq_len(n_year),
                   series = factor(species, levels = species))
dat$temp <- temp[dat$time]
dat$wind <- round(runif(nrow(dat)), 2)
dat$N <- N[cbind(dat$time, as.integer(dat$series))]

# Each individual present is counted with probability p, which falls
# with wind speed
p <- plogis(det_sp[dat$series] - 1.5 * dat$wind)
dat$y <- rbinom(nrow(dat), dat$N, p)

# Upper bound of the sum over N in each closure unit
dat$cap <- 80L
head(dat)
#>   visit time series temp wind  N  y cap
#> 1     1    1   sp_1 1.07 0.77 59 25  80
#> 2     2    1   sp_1 1.07 0.14 59 31  80
#> 3     3    1   sp_1 1.07 0.50 59 28  80
#> 4     4    1   sp_1 1.07 0.04 59 47  80
#> 5     5    1   sp_1 1.07 0.36 59 27  80
#> 6     1    2   sp_1 1.56 0.20 48 21  80

Each row is one visit. series names the species and time the year. The visits that share a (series, time) pair form one closure unit, over which NN is fixed. cap bounds the sum over NN in each unit. It must be at least the unit’s largest count. The model cannot estimate an abundance above it. The simulated abundances peak at 64, which leaves room below a cap of 80. Each unit of cap adds a term to the sum in every closure unit at every iteration. The N column holds the simulated abundance for comparison. The model never sees it.

The last three years are held out to score a forecast:

train <- subset(dat, time <= 17)
test <- subset(dat, time > 17)

Fitting the model

To estimate abundance and detection together, we put one formula on each inside bf(). The first describes abundance. The second, p ~, describes detection. trend_formula describes the latent log-abundance. In it, by = lv_axis() gives each species its own smooth of temperature. AR() gives each species its own AR(1) state:

mod <- mvgam(
  bf(y ~ series, p ~ series + wind),
  trend_formula = ~ s(temp, by = lv_axis(), k = 5) + AR(),
  data = train,
  newdata = test,
  family = nmix(),
  chains = 4, seed = 11, silent = 2
)
summary(mod)

The wind coefficient p_wind is -1.38 [-1.64, -1.15] on the logit scale, against the simulated value of −1.5-1.5.

Latent abundance

hindcast(type = "latent_state") returns the posterior of NN in each closure unit, conditional on the counts observed there. Its plot() method returns a ggplot, to which we add the simulated abundances and the largest count of each year:

hc <- hindcast(mod, type = "latent_state")
truth <- unique(train[, c("series", "time", "N")])
counts <- aggregate(y ~ series + time, data = train, FUN = max)
plot(hc) +
  geom_point(data = counts, aes(x = time, y = y), shape = 21,
             fill = "white", colour = "grey30", size = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = truth, aes(x = time, y = N), size = 1.6)

Posterior medians with 50% and 95% credible intervals of each species’ abundance. Black points are the simulated abundances. Open circles are the largest count in each year.

Because detection is imperfect, every count falls below the abundance it came from. The posterior median of NN exceeds the largest count in 65 of the 68 species-years. Its 95% intervals contain the simulated abundance in 68 of them. A model of the counts alone would report every population as smaller than it is.

Covariate effects

conditional_effects() accepts the N-mixture prediction types. With type = "latent_state" it draws the expected abundance against temperature. series = "all" gives each species its own panel:

plot(
  conditional_effects(mod, effects = "temp", type = "latent_state",
                      series = "all"),
  ask = FALSE
)

Expected abundance of each species against temperature, with 95% credible intervals.

The four smooths take the shapes we simulated: a saturating rise, a hump, a decline and a shallow U. With type = "detection", conditional_effects() draws the detection probability against wind speed:

plot(conditional_effects(mod, effects = "wind", type = "detection"),
     ask = FALSE)

Detection probability against wind speed, with its 95% credible interval.

Forecasts

forecast() advances each species’ AR(1) state through the held-out years. It combines the state with the temperature smooths and passes the result through detection. The forecast is of the count on each held-out visit:

fc <- forecast(mod)
plot(fc)

Counts predicted on each visit over the training years and the three held-out years. Points are the observed counts.

score() evaluates the forecast against the held-out counts. The forecast evaluation article compares models on such scores.

Checking the fit

To test whether the model reproduces the variation among visits, pp_check(type = "fit_stat") sums the counts of each closure unit. It measures their discrepancy from the expected sum with the chi-squared statistic of MacKenzie and Bailey (2004). It repeats the calculation on counts replicated from the posterior:

fit_stat <- pp_check(mod, type = "fit_stat")
fit_stat
#> Posterior predictive check (closure-unit discrepancy)
#>   Family:           nmix
#>   Statistic:        chi-squared
#>   Aggregation:      closure unit
#>   Posterior draws:  500
#>   Bayesian p-value: 0.394

A Bayesian p-value near 0 would mean the replicates rarely reach the discrepancy of the observed counts. The value here, 0.39, gives no sign of lack of fit. latent_N_saturation() reports the posterior probability that NN reaches the cap in each unit:

sat <- latent_N_saturation(mod)
max(sat$p_saturated)
#> [1] 0.017

The largest probability any unit gives to reaching the cap of 80 is 0.017.

Other observation processes

The binomial observation process assumes each individual present is detected independently on each visit. nmix() offers two more through its type argument. All three marginalise the latent abundance in the same way. Every method used above works with each of them.

Variant Constructor Response Detection
Poisson-binomial (Royle 2004) nmix() Counts that cannot exceed NN Probability pp per individual and visit, logit link
Royle-Nichols (Royle and Nichols 2003) nmix("royle_nichols") Detection or non-detection Probability rr per individual. A visit detects the species with probability 1−(1−r)N1 - (1 - r)^N
Poisson-Poisson nmix("poisson_poisson") Counts that can record one individual more than once Encounter rate pp per individual and visit, log link

Summary

From five counts a year, the N-mixture model recovered abundances that the counts alone understate. Its 95% intervals covered the simulated abundance in 68 of 68 species-years. The same fit recovered four differently shaped responses to temperature and the wind effect on detection. Because the abundance follows an mvgam trend, the fit also forecast the held-out counts. All of this came from one mvgam() call with family = nmix(), whose observation formula describes detection while its trend formula describes the latent abundance.

Where to next

Each function used here has a help page, such as ?nmix or ?latent_N_saturation, with its arguments and output. ?nmix gives the identification conditions and default priors of each variant. pivot_detection_array() converts detection arrays from unmarked, spOccupancy or ubms into the long format used here. occ() fits occupancy models to the same layout. how_to_cite() writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model, citing the N-mixture variant it used. methods_md() writes out its equations.
